transcript.text: induction hob keeps turnin off after 5-10 mins on high, have to keep restartin it. drives me nuts. any1 know y?

It is most often the hob’s overheat protection stepping in. Running on high for a while creates a lot of heat; if the ventilation underneath is restricted, the cooling fan is not doing its job, or a pan is making the zone work unusually hard, the hob may shut a zone down until it cools. 1. Let it cool fully, then check the pan: use a magnetic pan with a flat base that matches the marked zone. Avoid an empty pan or a small pan on a large zone. If it only happens with one pan, the pan/heat load is the likely trigger.
2. With the hob switched off and isolated at its wall switch/fused spur, make sure the air vents around the worktop/cupboard below are not blocked by utensils, foil, towels or stored items. Do not remove the hob or any covers.
3. Try a different zone and, if possible, a different suitable pan. One zone cutting out points more towards that zone’s sensor/power section; all zones or the whole hob points more towards cooling/ventilation or the main control system. A brief reduction in power on high can be normal on some induction hobs, but fully turning off after 5–10 minutes and needing a restart is not something to ignore if it happens repeatedly. When it cuts out, is it one cooking zone or the whole hob, and does the display show any letter/number or error symbol?
mostly the big front zones on high/boost. sometimes a code flashes up but too quick to read. fan roars before it cuts out. started when a new drawer unit went in under it a month ago

The new drawer unit is the strongest clue. The fan roaring suggests the hob is trying to cool itself, but the large front zones on high/Boost are likely overheating because the drawer or its contents are restricting the airflow underneath. This is much more likely than a failed zone, particularly as it began after the installation. 1. Let the hob cool, then isolate it at the wall switch/fused spur. Open the top drawer and check whether it sits very close to the underside of the hob, and whether cutlery trays, foil, utensils or stored items could block any gap or ventilation openings. Do not remove the hob or its covers. A clear gap with unobstructed airflow is needed; if the drawer has effectively boxed in the underside, the installer may need to alter it to the hob maker’s fitting requirements. 2. As a simple confirmation, on a cool hob try cooking with the top drawer fully open and empty, using a suitable large pan on one front zone at high — only while attended. If it now stays on longer, that suggests insufficient cabinet ventilation. Do not rely on this as the permanent fix. 3. If the flashing code reappears, a phone video may catch it. The exact code matters: an error affecting several zones supports an overheat/cooling issue, while one front zone alone would make that zone’s sensor or power module more suspect. If airflow is clear and it still shuts down with the drawer open, arrange a hob engineer: the cooling fan may be running but not moving enough air, or the temperature sensor/control electronics may be misreading heat. Avoid repeatedly restarting it on Boost until the ventilation issue is resolved.
not pulling the drawer out or touching under the hob. can i just try it with the drawer open instead? it does work again after a few mins cooling btw

Yes — trying it with the drawer fully open is a sensible, non-invasive test. You do not need to remove the drawer or touch underneath the hob. The fan noise is normal while it is trying to shed heat; the key question is whether the new drawer arrangement is trapping that heat. 1. Start with the hob cool. Empty the top drawer and leave it fully open.
2. Use a suitable large, flat induction pan on one of the affected front zones. Run it at the same high setting that normally causes the cut-out, while staying with it.
3. If it now runs substantially longer or does not cut out, the drawer/cabinet ventilation is very likely the cause. The permanent remedy is for the drawer installer or kitchen fitter to alter the installation so it meets the hob manufacturer’s required clearance and airflow — do not treat an open drawer as the long-term solution.
4. A cooling fan that runs but is not shifting enough air, or a temperature-sensor/control fault, becomes more likely and needs a hob engineer. Avoid repeatedly restarting it on Boost after it trips; let it cool properly first. If the quick flashing code appears again, a phone video of the display could help an engineer identify whether it is a general overheat fault or a zone-specific one.
ok will try it with the drawer open. what if it still cuts out?

If it still cuts out with the top drawer fully open and empty, do not keep restarting it on Boost. That result makes the drawer installation less conclusive and raises the likelihood of a cooling fault within the hob — most commonly a fan that runs but is not shifting enough air — or a temperature-sensor/control fault. It would then be sensible to book an induction-hob engineer. Tell them it cuts out after 5–10 minutes on high, the fan becomes very loud, it recovers after cooling, and a brief code sometimes appears. A short phone video of the display when it trips may capture the code and save diagnostic time. If it runs noticeably longer with the drawer open, the likely remedy is for the kitchen fitter/installer to provide the required clearance and ventilation beneath the hob; an open drawer is only a test, not a permanent solution. After you have tried it, does it still cut out at about the same time with the drawer fully open and empty?
haven't tried yet, will do it later. if it still cuts out i'll get an engineer then

That is a sensible plan. The cool-down recovery and loud fan make overheating protection the leading explanation; the drawer-open test should separate restricted cabinet airflow from a fault inside the hob. If it still cuts out with the drawer fully open and empty, book an induction-hob engineer rather than repeatedly restarting it. The likely areas for them to check are the cooling fan’s actual airflow, temperature sensing and the control/power electronics. If you can safely catch the brief code on a phone video when it happens, keep that for the engineer—it may shorten the diagnosis. If it runs properly with the drawer open, go back to the drawer/kitchen installer to correct the clearance and ventilation below the hob. The open drawer is only a diagnostic test, not a permanent workaround.

candidates: Overheating protection from restricted ventilation or a cooling fan problem (high)
Pan/base or very high-power cooking conditions causing a zone to protect itself (medium)
